Bender

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a contest: little shapes spin at the corners of a bigger one and fool your eyes.
How to play: Drag the marked corner to turn the picture, or the middle dot to move it. Change the choices, press Start to spin, and press Check the pattern when you want to test it.
Look for the math

The shape in the middle never moves. The little shapes at its corners do, and their motion makes perfectly straight sides look bent or even curved. Nothing is actually bent: the picture is exactly the same kind of regular polygon at every frame.

Where every corner is

Put the centre at C and let the big shape have n corners. Its corners are C + R·(cos(a + 2πk/n), sin(a + 2πk/n)) for k = 0, 1, …, n−1, where R is one third of the shorter side of the picture (rounded down to a whole pixel, as in the old Java code) and a is the angle set by the marked corner. Equal steps around a circle: that is all a regular polygon is.

The applet used four choices for the big shape (3, 4, 5 or 6 corners) and the same four for the little ones. Its size slider runs from 0 to 80, its speed slider from 0 to 200 — the pause is 200 − slider milliseconds — and its colour slider from 0 to 100 percent green.

All the little shapes turn together

At corner k, a small regular polygon with m corners and radius s has vertices Vk + s·(cos(π/m + 2πj/m + 2πk/n), sin(π/m + 2πj/m + 2πk/n)). At step I of the applet's 100 steps, every one of them is turned through the same angle 2πI/100 about its own corner. So all the small shapes stay alike, and turning the whole picture by 360°/n about C carries it onto itself — rotational symmetry survives every frame. The logic test checks this for all 4 × 4 pairs of shapes, all 81 sizes, all 100 steps and both modes.

The displaced setting

Ticked, the old applet's checkbox moved each small shape a little way off its corner. Reading the bytecode, the shift puts the midpoint of the shape's first edge two units farther out along the radius through that corner. The code rounded the shape to whole pixels before shifting it, so the symmetry can be off by a few pixels; the test allows that. The control here is named for what it does, because the original checkbox said "Centered" while ticking it switched the displaced mode on.

What is really an illusion

The page says the sides can seem misoriented, that a hexagon can look round, and that a triangle is the least troublesome big shape but the most useful little one. Those are claims about what people see, not about the points: the illusion is in the eye, and the geometry never breaks its rules. The original hexagon with six small triangles was invented by Walter Gerbino; try that pair with the shift turned on. The logic test does not try to measure how convincing an illusion looks.

Try a hexagon with six triangles as the spinning shapes, then press One step slowly and watch the red sides appear to tilt.
